etymologies.etymologyHTML: From New Latin microscopium and Italian microscopio, from Ancient Greek μικρός (mikrós, “small”) + σκοπέω (skopéō, “I look at”), equivalent to micro- +‎ -scope.

definitions.definition: An optical instrument used for observing small objects.

quote.citation: 1837, The Edinburgh New Philosophical Journal, volume 23, page 222:
quote.text: That he might ascertain whether any of the cloths of ancient Egypt were made of hemp, M. Dutrochet has examined with the microscope the weavable filaments of this last vegetable.

quote.citation: 1978, Jan Romein, The Watershed of Two Eras: Europe in 1900, page 303:
quote.text: Elsewhere, professionals could enthuse over new precision instruments capable, for instance, of measuring weights down to a tenth of a milligram, or over a host of self-registering thermometers and barometers, microscopes, typewriters, calculators and all sorts of technical and musical devices, including automatic concertinas, edeophones, auto-harps, bigophones and other long-forgotten objects.

definitions.definition: Any instrument for imaging very small objects (such as an electron microscope).
To examine with a microscope, to put under a microscope (literally or figuratively).

quote.text: It has a strong germicidal action, as can be verified by staining and microscoping the pus, the characteristic micro-organisms disappearing rapidly under its use.

quote.citation: 2012, E.J. Zingg, D.M.A. Wallace, Bladder Cancer, Springer Science & Business Media, →ISBN, page 79:
quote.text: Wright (1959), using the standard and less laborious technique of microscoping the centrifuged deposit of a sample of urine, found that 21.6% of males attending life insurance examinations had more than 10 red blood cells per high power field (rbc/hpf).
